title: Variables
summary: Give a **value** a name, and tell Java what kind of value it will hold.
refresher: A Java **variable** has a type, a name, and usually a **value**. In `int score = 10;`, `int` says the variable holds whole numbers, `score` is the name, and `10` is the starting value. Later assignments must still fit the declared type.

assign-01.title: Reassignment replaces the old value
assign-01.body: A variable holds the latest value assigned to that name. A later assignment overwrites the earlier one.
assign-01.notice: Trace assignments in order from top to bottom.
assign-01.mistake: Do not add old and new values together unless the code explicitly does that.

update-01.title: The right side runs first
update-01.body: An update like `count = count + 3` reads the old value first, computes the new value, then stores it.
update-01.notice: Write the old value beside the variable before applying the update.
update-01.mistake: Do not replace both sides at the same time in your head.

swap-01.title: Copies do not preserve overwritten values
swap-01.body: Assignment copies a value at that moment. If the original value is overwritten, it is gone unless another name saved it first.
swap-01.notice: A real swap needs a temporary save or a language-specific swap pattern.
swap-01.mistake: Do not assume two assignments automatically trade values.

name-01.title: Variable names follow naming rules
name-01.body: Names can use letters, digits, and underscores, but they cannot start with a digit.
name-01.notice: Ask whether the first character is legal before checking the rest.
name-01.mistake: Do not reject underscores just because they look unusual.

undefined-01.title: Names must exist before use
undefined-01.body: The program runs in order. A name created later is not available to an earlier line.
undefined-01.notice: For runtime name errors, find the first line that tries to read the missing name.
undefined-01.mistake: Do not assume a later assignment reaches backward in time.

typein-01.title: Trace the value after every line
typein-01.body: For final-value questions, keep a small table of the variable after each update.
typein-01.notice: The printed value is whatever the variable holds at the final output line.
typein-01.mistake: Do not skip middle updates because the starting value looks simple.

compound-update-01.title: Shorthand updates still use current state
compound-update-01.body: Compound assignment means update the variable using the value it already stores.
compound-update-01.notice: Apply each shorthand operation in order and replace the stored value each time.
compound-update-01.mistake: Do not treat `+=` or `*=` as separate values waiting until the end.

copy-value-01.title: A copied value stays copied
copy-value-01.body: After one variable receives another variable's value, later reassignment of the original name does not replay old lines.
copy-value-01.notice: Assignment is an event, not a live connection for simple values.
copy-value-01.mistake: Do not update the copied variable just because the source variable changed later.

shadow-scope-01.title: Local names can hide outer names
shadow-scope-01.body: A name created inside a function or method can be separate from a name outside it.
shadow-scope-01.notice: Track which scope the code is currently running in.
shadow-scope-01.mistake: Do not assume changing an inside name changes the outside name.

static-vs-dynamic-01.title: Type rules depend on the language
static-vs-dynamic-01.body: Some languages let a name later hold a different kind of value, while typed languages require a compatible type.
static-vs-dynamic-01.notice: Read the declaration or assignment rule for the selected language before predicting behavior.
static-vs-dynamic-01.mistake: Do not transfer Python or JavaScript habits directly into Java or C++.

sections.title: Declare a typed variable
sections.summary: Java variables start with a type, a name, and a value.

blocks.body: A **variable** is a name for a **value**. Java adds one extra step: before the name, you say what kind of value belongs there. That type is a promise. If you say `int`, Java expects whole numbers in that variable.

blocks.caption: Each **variable** says its type first. Java checks those types before the program runs.

blocks.body: The equals sign assigns a **value**. It does not ask whether two things are equal. Read `score = score + 5` as: take the old score, add five, and store the new result back in score.

sections.title: Reassign without changing type
sections.summary: The stored value can change, but the declared type stays put.

blocks.caption: A **variable** can change, but the new **value** still has to fit the type Java was promised.

blocks.title: The type stays for life
blocks.body: After you declare a **variable**, its type stays the same. An `int score` can receive another whole number later, but it cannot later hold text like `"ten"`.

blocks.title: The equals sign gives an order, it does not state a fact
blocks.body: In math, `x = 5` claims that x is 5. In Java it commands: put 5 into x. That is why `count = count + 1;` is not a contradiction. Java reads the right side first, gets whatever `count` holds at that moment, adds one, and stores the result back under the same name. The `==` you meet later is the one that asks whether two **values** match. A single `=` never asks. It puts.

blocks.caption: Reassignment needs no type, because the type was settled at the declaration. Writing `int count = 2;` on the third line would ask for a brand new **variable** rather than updating this one.

blocks.why: Take the lines in order, which is how Java takes them. `total` starts at 5. The second line makes it 5 + 3, so 8. The third doubles that 8, so 16. Picking 13 means the multiply got applied to the original 5 instead of the 8 that was sitting there by then. Each line works on the **value** the line above it left behind.

sections.title: Constants and naming habits
sections.summary: Use final values and readable Java names when the meaning matters.

blocks.body: Some **values** should be fixed the moment they are **set**: the credit cap on a full course load, a tax rate, the width of a board. Mark those `final`. The compiler then rejects any later attempt to assign to them, including your own.

blocks.caption: `final` gives a name one **value** and holds it there. Adding `MAX_CREDITS = 21;` below would fail with `cannot assign a value to final variable MAX_CREDITS`. That is the point of it: the error lands at compile time, before the program can act on a number nobody meant to change.

blocks.title: How Java programmers name things
items: Start lowercase, then capitalize the first letter of each new word. No spaces, no dashes.
A `final` constant is the **exception** to camelCase: capitals joined by underscores, as in `MAX_CREDITS` or `TAX_RATE`. The shape itself signals that the **value** never moves.
Capitalization is part of the name. `score` and `Score` refer to two separate **variables**.
Digits are allowed inside a name but not at the front: `score2` compiles, `2score` does not.
Spell out the contents. A reader can guess what `studentCount` holds. Nobody can guess `n`.

sections.title: Initialize before reading
sections.summary: Check the mistakes Java catches before your program runs.

blocks.title: Declaring is not the same as initializing
blocks.body: `int score;` reserves room for a number without putting one there. Read it before you assign to it and the compiler stops you with `variable score might not have been initialized`. Java would rather refuse to build than hand you a number nobody chose. The usual fix is to declare and assign on one line, which is why most Java you come across does both at once.

blocks.caption: Both sides declare `score` as an `int`. The right side gives it a **value** before reading it. The left side is not a crash partway through a run: it never runs, because javac produces no **class** **file** to run.

blocks.body: The compiler catches one more thing early: the same name declared twice in one block. Once `score` exists, the name is taken. Writing `int` in front of it again asks for a second **variable** under a name that is already spoken for.

blocks.prompt: What happens when you compile and run this?
choices: It fails to compile: score is already defined
It prints 10, then crashes while running
blocks.why: The third line declares `score` a second time in a block that already has one, so javac reports `variable score is already defined in method main(String[])` and produces nothing to run. Dropping that second `int` and writing `score = 20;` is what gives you 10 then 20, because that reassigns the **variable** instead of declaring a new one. Note that no **output** appears at all here, not even the first 10: a compile error stops the program before its first line runs.

blocks.body: That is the trade Java offers. It asks for a type on every declaration and a **value** in every **local variable** before you read it. In exchange it catches a whole family of mistakes while the **file** is still open in your editor, rather than while someone is running the program.

blocks.title: Before you move on
items: Put the type before the name.
Pick names that say what the **value** means.
Use == later when you want to compare.
Keep the **value** compatible with the declared type.
